title: Invasive Species and Food-Web Changes Core Test
description: Distinguish introduced species from harmful invaders, trace direct and indirect food-web effects, and evaluate evidence for management choices.

questions.prompt: A species is introduced outside its natural range. Is that fact alone enough to call it invasive?
questions.questionText: A species is introduced outside its natural range. Is that fact alone enough to call it invasive?
options: Yes; every introduced species is necessarily invasive.
No; plants can never be invasive.
No; evidence of harm or likely harm is also needed.
Yes; geographic origin alone proves ecological damage.
questions.correctAnswer: No; evidence of harm or likely harm is also needed.
questions.explanation: Non-native and invasive are not interchangeable; harm or likely harm is part of the definition.

questions.prompt: A new non-native plant shades native seedlings and spreads through a habitat. Which observation most directly documents an environmental impact?
questions.questionText: A new non-native plant shades native seedlings and spreads through a habitat. Which observation most directly documents an environmental impact?
options: The plant has an unfamiliar name.
The plant grows on a different continent from its origin.
Native seedling survival is lower where its dense cover blocks light.
The plant has flowers a visitor finds attractive.
questions.correctAnswer: Native seedling survival is lower where its dense cover blocks light.
questions.explanation: Measured effects on native seedlings provide impact evidence; novelty or appearance does not.

questions.prompt: In native plant -> insect -> bird, an introduced herbivore eats the native plant. What indirect effect could follow?
questions.questionText: In native plant -> insect -> bird, an introduced herbivore eats the native plant. What indirect effect could follow?
options: Bird food may decrease if insects lose their host plants.
Every bird must immediately increase.
The herbivore directly eats the bird in this model.
The native plant receives more sunlight from being eaten.
questions.correctAnswer: Bird food may decrease if insects lose their host plants.
questions.explanation: Effects can pass through host plants and insects to birds, even without direct interaction.

questions.prompt: Why can an introduced predator sometimes have a large effect in a new habitat?
questions.questionText: Why can an introduced predator sometimes have a large effect in a new habitat?
options: Every introduced predator has unlimited energy.
Local prey may have few effective defenses against it.
Introduced predators never need suitable conditions.
All native prey must be identical.
questions.correctAnswer: Local prey may have few effective defenses against it.
questions.explanation: Local interactions and defenses influence impact; introduction does not guarantee success.

questions.prompt: What is a food-web prediction rather than a measured observation?
questions.questionText: What is a food-web prediction rather than a measured observation?
options: Native fish may decline if an introduced fish consumes much of their shared food.
A survey counted 18 native fish.
A sample contained 12 introduced fish.
A sensor recorded a water temperature of 16 degrees Celsius.
questions.correctAnswer: Native fish may decline if an introduced fish consumes much of their shared food.
questions.explanation: A prediction describes an expected outcome; counts and sensor readings are observations.

questions.prompt: A native species becomes very abundant. Does abundance alone make it a non-native invasive species?
questions.questionText: A native species becomes very abundant. Does abundance alone make it a non-native invasive species?
options: Yes; any large population is non-native.
Yes; all common species are invasive.
No; abundance alone does not establish non-native origin or harm.
No; a native species can never affect other organisms.
questions.correctAnswer: No; abundance alone does not establish non-native origin or harm.
questions.explanation: Origin, context, and impact must be considered separately from abundance.

questions.prompt: A non-native plant occupies 10 of 50 sampled plots. What fraction of sampled plots contains it?
questions.questionText: A non-native plant occupies 10 of 50 sampled plots. What fraction of sampled plots contains it?
options: One half.
Four fifths.
One fifth.
One tenth.
questions.correctAnswer: One fifth.
questions.explanation: 10 out of 50 simplifies to one fifth. Occupancy does not by itself quantify harm.

questions.prompt: Which comparison best tests whether an introduced competitor affects native plant growth?
questions.questionText: Which comparison best tests whether an introduced competitor affects native plant growth?
options: Matched plots with and without its presence, similar starting conditions, and repeated growth measurements.
One invaded sunny plot versus one uninvaded shaded plot measured once.
Photographs from different seasons without plot sizes.
Only the introduced plant's height.
questions.correctAnswer: Matched plots with and without its presence, similar starting conditions, and repeated growth measurements.
questions.explanation: Matched comparisons and repeated measurements help separate its effect from other environmental differences.

questions.prompt: A non-native aquatic plant forms a dense surface mat. Which pathway could reduce submerged plant growth?
questions.questionText: A non-native aquatic plant forms a dense surface mat. Which pathway could reduce submerged plant growth?
options: Surface mat -> more underwater light -> less photosynthesis.
Surface mat -> less underwater light -> less photosynthesis.
Surface mat -> submerged plants stop needing carbon dioxide.
Surface mat -> water molecules become sunlight.
questions.correctAnswer: Surface mat -> less underwater light -> less photosynthesis.
questions.explanation: Shading can change a resource used by submerged producers.

questions.prompt: Why should a model include native competitors as well as an introduced species?
questions.questionText: Why should a model include native competitors as well as an introduced species?
options: Native organisms cannot interact with introduced ones.
Only introduced species need resources.
Competition always guarantees the introduced species disappears.
They can alter its access to resources and the resulting impact.
questions.correctAnswer: They can alter its access to resources and the resulting impact.
questions.explanation: Outcome depends on interactions and resource limits, not origin alone.

questions.prompt: A site gains a new species but loses three native species. What happened to its species count?
questions.questionText: A site gains a new species but loses three native species. What happened to its species count?
options: It increased by one.
It decreased by two.
It stayed the same.
It decreased by four.
questions.correctAnswer: It decreased by two.
questions.explanation: Adding one and losing three gives a net change of minus two.

questions.prompt: An introduced organism survives near a warm outlet but not in colder nearby water. What does this show?
questions.questionText: An introduced organism survives near a warm outlet but not in colder nearby water. What does this show?
options: Introduction guarantees success in all habitats.
Environmental conditions can limit establishment or persistence.
Cold water has no role in population patterns.
The organism must be native at the warm site.
questions.correctAnswer: Environmental conditions can limit establishment or persistence.
questions.explanation: Suitable conditions matter, and local success does not predict success everywhere.

questions.prompt: A student says an invasive species must eat native organisms. Which response is best?
questions.questionText: A student says an invasive species must eat native organisms. Which response is best?
options: Only predators can be invasive.
Plant species cannot change habitat.
Competition always benefits both species.
Harm can also occur through competition or habitat changes.
questions.correctAnswer: Harm can also occur through competition or habitat changes.
questions.explanation: Invasive impacts can involve several mechanisms, including shading and resource depletion.

questions.prompt: A model includes introduced plant -> fewer native plants -> fewer specialist insects. Which link needs evidence to support the insect prediction?
questions.questionText: A model includes introduced plant -> fewer native plants -> fewer specialist insects. Which link needs evidence to support the insect prediction?
options: That the insects depend on the affected native plants.
That the introduced plant has green leaves.
That both plant names appear in a guide.
That the survey took place in daylight.
questions.correctAnswer: That the insects depend on the affected native plants.
questions.explanation: The indirect prediction depends on a real feeding relationship, not just plant presence.

questions.prompt: Native fish counts fell after a species arrived, but water temperature also rose. What should investigators check?
questions.questionText: Native fish counts fell after a species arrived, but water temperature also rose. What should investigators check?
options: Whether arrival must be the only cause because it came first.
Whether fish counts are irrelevant to impact.
Whether the temperature readings should be discarded.
Whether warming could explain some of the decline.
questions.correctAnswer: Whether warming could explain some of the decline.
questions.explanation: Several changes can coincide; alternative causes need consideration.

questions.prompt: An introduced filter feeder reduces suspended food particles. Which native organisms might be affected first through food competition?
questions.questionText: An introduced filter feeder reduces suspended food particles. Which native organisms might be affected first through food competition?
options: Only organisms that never use water.
Native organisms that also feed on those particles.
All tree species equally regardless of habitat.
Only top predators with no food-web connection.
questions.correctAnswer: Native organisms that also feed on those particles.
questions.explanation: Competition is strongest evidence-wise when the shared resource and users are identified.

questions.prompt: Before arrival a site had 60 native individuals; later it had 36. What is the measured decline?
questions.questionText: Before arrival a site had 60 native individuals; later it had 36. What is the measured decline?
options: 36 individuals.
60 individuals.
96 individuals.
24 individuals.
questions.correctAnswer: 24 individuals.
questions.explanation: 60 - 36 = 24; this measures change but does not isolate its cause.

questions.prompt: Why might removing an invasive plant not immediately restore a habitat?
questions.questionText: Why might removing an invasive plant not immediately restore a habitat?
options: Removal always restores every food-web link instantly.
Native plants do not need resources after removal.
Soil conditions, missing native plants, or other limiting factors may remain.
No monitoring is useful once the target is gone.
questions.correctAnswer: Soil conditions, missing native plants, or other limiting factors may remain.
questions.explanation: Removing one pressure does not automatically replace missing habitat components.

questions.prompt: Two plans reduce invasive cover equally. Plan A also damages many native plants; Plan B largely avoids them. Which ecological criterion favors B?
questions.questionText: Two plans reduce invasive cover equally. Plan A also damages many native plants; Plan B largely avoids them. Which ecological criterion favors B?
options: Lower non-target damage.
A shorter plan name.
More equipment regardless of effect.
Larger total disturbance regardless of outcome.
questions.correctAnswer: Lower non-target damage.
questions.explanation: Target reduction should be evaluated alongside effects on organisms being protected.

questions.prompt: A food-web diagram uses arrows from food to consumer. Which arrow represents an introduced fish eating native insects?
questions.questionText: A food-web diagram uses arrows from food to consumer. Which arrow represents an introduced fish eating native insects?
options: Native insects -> introduced fish.
Introduced fish -> native insects.
Sunlight -> introduced fish directly.
Native fish -> sunlight.
questions.correctAnswer: Native insects -> introduced fish.
questions.explanation: Food-to-consumer arrows show the direction of matter and energy transfer.

questions.prompt: Invaded plots lose 30 native plants; matched uninvaded plots lose 20 during the same drought. What comparison is justified?
questions.questionText: Invaded plots lose 30 native plants; matched uninvaded plots lose 20 during the same drought. What comparison is justified?
options: The introduced species certainly caused all 30 losses.
The invaded plots lost 10 more, while shared drought effects may contribute.
The introduced species caused exactly 20 losses.
Drought had no possible effect because both groups were counted.
questions.correctAnswer: The invaded plots lost 10 more, while shared drought effects may contribute.
questions.explanation: The excess loss is 10, but causal attribution still depends on study quality and other differences.

questions.prompt: An introduced prey species becomes food for one native predator while harming other natives. What conclusion is warranted?
questions.questionText: An introduced prey species becomes food for one native predator while harming other natives. What conclusion is warranted?
options: One predator benefit proves there can be no invasion impact.
Any negative effect proves no native organism can benefit.
Every food-web member must respond in the same direction.
A benefit to one species does not rule out wider harm.
questions.correctAnswer: A benefit to one species does not rule out wider harm.
questions.explanation: Food-web effects can differ among organisms, so the whole outcome needs evaluation.

questions.prompt: A proposal releases a new predator to control an invader. What evidence is especially important before specialists consider release?
questions.questionText: A proposal releases a new predator to control an invader. What evidence is especially important before specialists consider release?
options: Whether its name is easy to remember.
Whether it is larger than the invader in every photograph.
Whether it can be released before any feeding studies.
Whether the predator could also harm native species or spread beyond the target area.
questions.correctAnswer: Whether the predator could also harm native species or spread beyond the target area.
questions.explanation: A control organism creates new interactions; non-target effects and spread need evaluation.

questions.prompt: A cleared site regains invasive cover from nearby untreated patches. Which model link was overlooked?
questions.questionText: A cleared site regains invasive cover from nearby untreated patches. Which model link was overlooked?
options: Movement of the target species into the site from surrounding sources.
Conversion of native plants into invasive plants.
Creation of sunlight by cleared soil.
Permanent closure of all habitat boundaries.
questions.correctAnswer: Movement of the target species into the site from surrounding sources.
questions.explanation: Management must consider the site within its surrounding landscape.

questions.prompt: A survey doubles the number of traps and catches twice as many introduced insects. Can it conclude the population doubled?
questions.questionText: A survey doubles the number of traps and catches twice as many introduced insects. Can it conclude the population doubled?
options: Yes; catches are independent of effort.
Yes; any larger count proves faster spread.
No; increased sampling effort can explain the larger catch.
No; traps can never provide population evidence.
questions.correctAnswer: No; increased sampling effort can explain the larger catch.
questions.explanation: Comparable effort or catch per unit effort is needed to interpret the trend.

questions.prompt: Which result best supports a treatment helping native plants?
questions.questionText: Which result best supports a treatment helping native plants?
options: The treatment removes visible invaders for one day.
The treatment uses the most expensive equipment.
Only the treated plot is photographed after rain.
Repeated treated plots show more native recovery than matched untreated plots, with low non-target damage.
questions.correctAnswer: Repeated treated plots show more native recovery than matched untreated plots, with low non-target damage.
questions.explanation: Recovery comparisons and harm measures evaluate both effectiveness and tradeoffs.

questions.prompt: A model predicts an introduced predator will reduce native prey. The predator instead eats mostly another introduced species. What should change?
questions.questionText: A model predicts an introduced predator will reduce native prey. The predator instead eats mostly another introduced species. What should change?
options: Keep the original diet assumption regardless of evidence.
Revise the feeding links and predictions using the observed diet.
Conclude all predators have the same effect everywhere.
Delete every native species from the model.
questions.correctAnswer: Revise the feeding links and predictions using the observed diet.
questions.explanation: Predictions depend on actual interactions; observed diet can require a model revision.

questions.prompt: Removal lowers invasive cover from 70% to 20%, while native cover rises from 15% to 25%. Which report is accurate?
questions.questionText: Removal lowers invasive cover from 70% to 20%, while native cover rises from 15% to 25%. Which report is accurate?
options: Both changed by 50 percentage points.
Invasive cover fell 50 percentage points; native cover rose 10 percentage points.
Native cover recovered to 70%.
The invasive plant is absent from the site.
questions.correctAnswer: Invasive cover fell 50 percentage points; native cover rose 10 percentage points.
questions.explanation: The two indicators show different changes, and 20% target cover remains.

questions.prompt: An unrecognized plant appears along a walking route. What is an appropriate investigation step?
questions.questionText: An unrecognized plant appears along a walking route. What is an appropriate investigation step?
options: Pull it out immediately because unfamiliar means invasive.
Move it to another park to compare growth.
Record a photo and location from a safe distance and seek reliable identification before judging impact.
Release a consumer nearby to test whether it is harmful.
questions.correctAnswer: Record a photo and location from a safe distance and seek reliable identification before judging impact.
questions.explanation: Identification and context come before action; moving or removing unknown organisms can cause harm.

questions.prompt: A report finds an introduced species spreading, native cover falling, and soil becoming drier. What conclusion best matches these observations alone?
questions.questionText: A report finds an introduced species spreading, native cover falling, and soil becoming drier. What conclusion best matches these observations alone?
options: There is reason to investigate impact, but the causal links need further evidence.
The introduced species has been proved to cause every change.
The spread proves all native organisms will disappear.
The observations prove there is no environmental harm.
questions.correctAnswer: There is reason to investigate impact, but the causal links need further evidence.
questions.explanation: These patterns justify investigation but do not yet isolate mechanisms or future outcomes.
